q: An LPN is assigned four patients. Which patient should the LPN check on first?
options: A patient who is 2 days post-op and stable, asking for pain medication
A patient who just returned from a walk and is now short of breath and anxious
A patient waiting for discharge teaching to be reinforced
A patient asking when their next meal will be served
rationale: A sudden new symptom (shortness of breath, anxiety) in a previously stable patient is a change in condition and must be checked first. The other patients have stable, expected needs.

q: Which task can the LPN safely delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
options: Teaching a patient how to use a new inhaler for the first time
Taking vital signs on a stable, established patient
Assessing a new patient who just arrived on the unit
Deciding whether a patient's pain medication order needs to be changed
rationale: Routine tasks with predictable outcomes on stable patients, like vital signs, can be delegated to UAP. Initial teaching, assessment of a new patient, and clinical decisions require a licensed nurse's judgment.

q: A patient asks the LPN to explain the risks of a surgery before signing the consent form. What should the LPN do?
options: Explain the risks as best as possible, since the LPN has heard the surgeon describe them before
Sign as a witness without any explanation
Tell the patient the surgeon needs to discuss this, and notify the surgeon of the patient's questions
Tell the patient not to worry, most surgeries like this go fine
rationale: Explaining the risks/benefits of a procedure is the responsibility of the provider performing it, not the nurse. The nurse should notify the provider so the patient's questions are fully answered before consenting.

q: An LPN believes a written order from a provider is unclear. What is the correct action?
options: Carry out the order using best judgment about what was probably meant
Ask a family member what they think the order means
Contact the prescriber to clarify the order before carrying it out
Skip that order and move to the next task
rationale: An unclear or unsafe order should always be clarified with the prescriber before it is carried out. Guessing at intent risks patient harm.

q: Under HIPAA, when is it appropriate for a nurse to discuss a patient's health information with another staff member?
options: Whenever another staff member on any unit asks out of curiosity
Only when that staff member is directly involved in the patient's care and needs the information
Freely, as long as it is discussed quietly
Only with the patient's immediate family, regardless of the staff member's role
rationale: HIPAA limits sharing of patient health information to those directly involved in that patient's care, and only the information they need for that care.

q: A nurse realizes she gave a patient the wrong dose of a medication. What is the first thing she should do?
options: Complete an incident report immediately, before anything else
Check on the patient's condition and notify the RN or provider right away
Wait to see if the patient develops any symptoms before doing anything
Document the correct dose in the chart to fix the record
rationale: Patient safety comes first: assess the patient and notify the RN/provider immediately. The incident report is completed afterward as a separate quality and safety record.

q: What is the purpose of using SBAR when reporting a change in a patient's condition?
options: To decide whether the patient needs a new roommate
To give a clear, organized structure for communicating important information
To determine who delegated the task originally
To replace the need for writing in the patient's chart
rationale: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is a simple, standard structure that keeps a handoff or urgent report clear and complete.

q: Which patient is the most appropriate assignment for the LPN, working under RN supervision?
options: A patient who was just admitted with an unclear diagnosis
A patient in critical, rapidly changing condition
A patient recovering as expected, 3 days after a routine surgery
A patient whose condition is worsening quickly and unpredictably
rationale: The LPN's scope is best suited to stable patients with predictable, expected outcomes. New, unstable, or rapidly changing patients are generally the RN's assignment.

q: Which precaution should be used for every patient, regardless of their diagnosis?
options: Airborne precautions
Standard precautions
Droplet precautions
Contact precautions
rationale: Standard precautions (hand hygiene, gloves for body fluid contact, etc.) are used with every patient, every time, regardless of known infection status.

q: A patient has tuberculosis. What type of precautions are needed?
options: Contact precautions with gown and gloves
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask
Airborne precautions with an N95 respirator and a special room
Standard precautions only
rationale: Tuberculosis spreads through very small airborne particles, so it requires airborne precautions, including an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room.

q: What is the single most effective action to prevent the spread of infection in a healthcare setting?
options: Wearing gloves at all times
Hand hygiene before and after patient contact
Wearing a mask around every patient
Using antibacterial soap only, never hand sanitizer
rationale: Hand hygiene, performed consistently before and after every patient contact, remains the single most effective infection-prevention measure.

q: An older patient is confused and known to be a fall risk. Which action best supports their safety?
options: Leave the bed in a raised position for easier staff access
Keep the bed in the lowest position and the call light within reach
Encourage the patient to walk to the bathroom alone to build independence
Remove the call light so the patient is not tempted to get up alone
rationale: For a known fall risk, keeping the bed low and the call light within reach reduces injury risk if the patient tries to get up unassisted.

q: Before applying a physical restraint, what must the nurse confirm?
options: That the family has given verbal permission only
That a time-limited order has been obtained from a provider
That the patient has been restrained before without problems
That no other option needs to be tried first
rationale: A restraint always requires a time-limited provider order and is used only after less restrictive measures have failed — never for convenience or punishment.

q: What does the 'R' stand for in the fire safety mnemonic RACE?
options: Report
Rescue
Remove
Restrict
rationale: RACE stands for Rescue (anyone in immediate danger), Alarm, Confine, and Extinguish/Evacuate.

q: Which is the correct body mechanic principle when helping move a patient?
options: Bend at the waist and keep the patient at arm's length
Bend at the knees and keep the patient close to your body
Twist your spine while lifting to save time
Lift quickly to reduce the total time spent lifting
rationale: Proper body mechanics means bending at the knees (not the back), keeping a wide base of support, and keeping the load close to the body to prevent injury.

q: A patient has active shingles (herpes zoster) with draining lesions. Which precaution is appropriate in addition to standard precautions?
options: Droplet precautions only
Contact precautions
No additional precautions are needed
Reverse (protective) isolation only
rationale: Draining skin lesions spread by direct or indirect contact, so contact precautions (gown and gloves) are used in addition to standard precautions.

q: At what age do infants typically develop a social smile?
options: Birth to 2 weeks
6 to 8 weeks
6 to 8 months
12 months
rationale: A social smile — smiling in response to a person, not just reflexively — typically develops around 6 to 8 weeks of age.

q: What kind of play is typical for a toddler (1-3 years old)?
options: Cooperative play, working together on a shared goal
Parallel play, playing near but not directly with other children
Solitary play only, with no interest in other children present
Team-based, rule-following play
rationale: Toddlers typically engage in parallel play — playing alongside other children without direct interaction.

q: Which is an expected, normal change of aging, rather than a sign of illness?
options: Sudden confusion that appeared overnight
Gradually thinner skin and slightly slower reflexes
New chest pain with exertion
Sudden loss of vision in one eye
rationale: Thinner skin and somewhat slower reflexes are expected, gradual changes of normal aging. Sudden changes like new confusion, chest pain, or vision loss are not expected and need prompt evaluation.

q: Which finding in pregnancy should be reported to the provider promptly?
options: Mild fatigue in the first trimester
Decreased fetal movement
Occasional mild back discomfort
Slight swelling of the ankles at the end of the day
rationale: Decreased fetal movement is a warning sign that needs prompt evaluation. Mild fatigue, occasional back discomfort, and end-of-day ankle swelling are common and expected in pregnancy.

q: What is a normal respiratory rate range for a healthy newborn?
options: 12-20 breaths per minute
30-60 breaths per minute
60-100 breaths per minute
10-15 breaths per minute
rationale: A normal newborn respiratory rate is about 30-60 breaths per minute, faster than the normal adult range of 12-20.

q: The Apgar score, done at 1 and 5 minutes after birth, evaluates all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Heart rate (pulse)
Muscle tone (activity)
Blood glucose level
Reflex response (grimace)
rationale: Apgar evaluates Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, and Respiration. Blood glucose is not part of the Apgar score.

q: Which lifestyle habit is most appropriate general health-promotion advice for an adult of any age?
options: Regular exercise, balanced diet, adequate sleep, and not smoking
Avoiding all exercise to prevent injury
Skipping meals to reduce workload on digestion
Sleeping as little as possible to be more productive
rationale: Regular exercise, a balanced diet, adequate sleep, and avoiding tobacco form the foundation of general health-promotion counseling for adults of any age.

q: An adolescent (12-18 years) is developmentally focused mainly on:
options: Learning to walk and talk
Parallel play with peers
Forming a sense of identity
Toilet training
rationale: Adolescence is centered on forming identity (Erikson's identity vs. role confusion stage) and developing abstract thinking.

q: Which is an example of a therapeutic communication technique?
options: Asking the patient 'why did you do that?'
Reflecting the patient's own words back to them
Giving the patient advice on what they should do
Reassuring the patient that everything will be fine
rationale: Reflecting the patient's own words back invites them to say more and shows you're listening. Asking 'why,' giving advice, and false reassurance can shut down communication.

q: A patient says, 'I don't know how I'll cope after this diagnosis.' What is the best response?
options: 'Don't worry, plenty of people get through this fine.'
'Why do you feel that way?'
'That sounds really hard. Tell me more about what's worrying you.'
'You should talk to a counselor about that.'
rationale: Acknowledging the patient's feelings and inviting them to share more is therapeutic. False reassurance, 'why' questions, and quick advice tend to shut conversation down.

q: Which of the following is generally recognized as a stage of grief (though not always in a fixed order)?
options: Denial
Distraction
Delegation
Diagnosis
rationale: The commonly taught stages of grief are denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. People do not always move through them in order.

q: A patient tells the nurse they sometimes think about ending their life. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep it private since the patient asked not to worry anyone
Report it immediately to the RN or provider
Wait to see if the patient brings it up again before acting
Change the subject to avoid upsetting the patient further
rationale: Any statement about self-harm or suicide must always be taken seriously and reported immediately — it is never something to keep quiet or dismiss.

q: When abuse is suspected, what should the nurse do first?
options: Confront the suspected abuser directly
Ensure the immediate safety of the patient
Wait until the patient brings it up on their own
Ask leading questions to confirm the suspicion quickly
rationale: The first priority when abuse is suspected is always the patient's immediate safety, followed by careful, non-leading documentation and required reporting.

q: Which symptom pattern is most consistent with depression?
options: A single bad day with low energy
Persistent low mood or loss of interest most days for at least two weeks
Excitement and high energy lasting one week
Occasional worry before a big event
rationale: Depression involves a persistent low mood or loss of interest most of the day, most days, for at least two weeks, often with changes in sleep, appetite, and energy.

q: A nurse is documenting a statement from a patient who reports possible neglect. What is the best documentation practice?
options: Summarize the general idea of what the patient said in the nurse's own words
Write down the patient's exact words, in quotes, without adding interpretation
Skip documentation until a supervisor reviews the case
Only document if the nurse personally witnessed the neglect
rationale: Objective documentation using the patient's own words, without added interpretation, provides the clearest and most accurate record in suspected abuse or neglect cases.

q: Which position best helps a patient who is having trouble breathing?
options: Flat on their back (supine)
Semi-Fowler's, head of bed at 30-45 degrees
Trendelenburg, head lower than feet
Lying on the stomach (prone)
rationale: Semi-Fowler's and High Fowler's positions help the lungs expand more fully and are used for patients with breathing difficulty.

q: How often should a patient who cannot move on their own generally be repositioned to protect their skin?
options: Every 30 minutes
At least every 2 hours
Once per shift
Only when they ask to be moved
rationale: Repositioning at least every 2 hours is a standard guideline to prevent pressure injuries in patients who cannot reposition themselves.

q: A pressure injury shows intact skin with a red area that does not turn white when pressed. What stage is this?
options: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
rationale: Stage 1 pressure injuries have intact skin with non-blanchable redness — the skin is not yet broken.

q: A patient has a swallowing problem (dysphagia). Which mealtime practice is safest?
options: Lying flat while eating to relax the throat muscles
Sitting upright and using the ordered liquid consistency
Offering large bites to reduce the number of swallows needed
Rushing meals to reduce fatigue
rationale: Sitting upright and using the correctly thickened liquid consistency, along with small bites, reduces the risk of choking or aspiration in patients with dysphagia.

q: Where should a urinary catheter drainage bag be positioned?
options: Above the level of the bladder
Below the level of the bladder
At the same height as the bladder
Position does not matter as long as tubing is secure
rationale: Keeping the drainage bag below the level of the bladder allows urine to drain properly by gravity and helps prevent backflow and infection.

q: Which diet is most appropriate for a patient with heart failure and fluid retention?
options: High-sodium diet
Low-sodium diet
High-potassium diet
Low-fiber diet
rationale: A low-sodium diet helps reduce fluid retention, which is important for patients with heart failure and related blood pressure conditions.

q: What is a common complication of prolonged immobility?
options: Improved circulation
Pressure injuries and blood clots
Increased muscle strength
Improved digestion
rationale: Prolonged immobility increases the risk of pressure injuries, blood clots, pneumonia, constipation, and muscle weakness — the opposite of the incorrect options.

q: For constipation, which intervention should generally be tried first?
options: A strong laxative immediately
Increased fluids, fiber, and movement/walking
A stool softener before any other measure
No intervention is needed unless it lasts a month
rationale: Simple, low-risk measures — more fluids, more fiber, more movement — are tried first before moving to stool softeners or laxatives.

q: Which are the core 'Rights' of medication administration?
options: Right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time
Right patient, right doctor, right nurse, right hospital, right room
Right patient, right family, right insurance, right pharmacy, right shift
Right dose, right color, right size, right shape, right smell
rationale: The core Rights are right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, and right time, always checked before giving any medication.

q: Before giving any medication, what must the nurse always check first?
options: The patient's favorite food
The patient's known allergies
The patient's marital status
The patient's room number only
rationale: Checking for known allergies before giving any medication is a critical safety step to prevent an allergic reaction.

q: By what route is insulin most commonly given?
options: Oral (by mouth)
Intramuscular (into the muscle)
Subcutaneous (just under the skin)
Sublingual (under the tongue)
rationale: Insulin is most commonly given subcutaneously; sites are rotated within the same general body area to keep absorption predictable.

q: A patient receiving an opioid pain medication should be monitored closely for:
options: Increased appetite
Slowed breathing and excessive sleepiness
Improved energy
Faster heart rate only
rationale: Opioids can slow breathing and cause excessive sedation; the respiratory rate should be checked before giving another dose.

q: A patient on warfarin (a blood thinner) should be monitored for which sign?
options: Excessive hunger
Unusual bleeding or bruising
Improved wound healing
Increased blood clotting
rationale: Blood thinners like warfarin increase bleeding risk, so unusual bleeding or bruising is an important sign to monitor for and report.

q: A patient taking insulin develops sudden sweating, shakiness, and confusion. What does this most likely indicate?
options: High blood sugar (hyperglycemia)
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia)
An allergic reaction
Normal medication effect, no action needed
rationale: Sweating, shakiness, and confusion are classic signs of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), which needs fast treatment with a quick source of sugar.

q: What is the first step if the LPN realizes a medication error has occurred?
options: Complete the incident report before checking on the patient
Check on the patient's safety and notify the RN or provider right away
Wait to see if any symptoms develop before telling anyone
Correct the medication administration record only
rationale: Patient safety always comes first: check on the patient and notify the RN/provider immediately, then complete the required incident report.

q: A patient develops a rash and difficulty breathing shortly after a new antibiotic is given. What should the nurse do?
options: Wait 30 minutes to see if it resolves on its own
Stop and ensure the patient's safety, then notify the RN/provider immediately
Give the next scheduled dose as planned
Document it and mention it at the end of the shift
rationale: A new rash with difficulty breathing after a medication suggests a possible allergic reaction, which requires immediate action and prompt notification.

q: What is one of the most important signs to report immediately in any patient?
options: A stable, unchanged appetite
A new change in level of consciousness
A patient sleeping through the night
A patient's usual daily routine
rationale: A new change in level of consciousness (more confused, harder to wake, less responsive) often signals a serious, developing problem and should be reported immediately.

q: What is considered a normal adult resting heart rate?
options: 40-60 beats per minute
60-100 beats per minute
100-140 beats per minute
150-180 beats per minute
rationale: A normal adult resting heart rate is generally 60-100 beats per minute.

q: What is generally considered a fever in an adult?
options: 37.0 C (98.6 F) or higher
37.5 C (99.5 F) exactly, no higher or lower
38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher
39.5 C (103.1 F) or higher only
rationale: A fever in adults is generally defined as a temperature of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher.

q: After surgery, what is the first priority when checking on the patient?
options: Asking about their appetite
Airway and breathing
Their preference for room temperature
Reviewing their visitor list
rationale: After any procedure, airway and breathing are always the first priority, followed by circulation, then comfort and other needs.

q: Why is it important to encourage a post-surgical patient to turn, cough, and deep breathe regularly?
options: To help them fall asleep faster
To prevent pneumonia and support lung function
To reduce the need for pain medication
To speed up wound closure only
rationale: Turning, coughing, and deep breathing help prevent pneumonia and atelectasis (partial lung collapse) after surgery by keeping the lungs expanded.

q: What is a normal fasting blood glucose range for most adults?
options: 40-69 mg/dL
70-99 mg/dL
rationale: A normal fasting blood glucose is generally about 70-99 mg/dL.

q: A surgical dressing shows a growing area of bright red drainage. What should the LPN do?
options: Remove the dressing completely to inspect the wound directly
Reinforce or note the dressing and report the finding to the RN promptly
Ignore it since some drainage is always expected
Wait until the next scheduled dressing change
rationale: Increasing or bright red drainage should be reported promptly; the dressing is generally reinforced rather than removed unless instructed otherwise.

q: Which finding would be most important to report to the RN right away?
options: A stable patient asking for a blanket
A patient's oxygen saturation dropping from 97% to 88%
A patient requesting their usual lunch tray
A patient asking what time visiting hours end
rationale: A significant drop in oxygen saturation (from 97% to 88%) is a concerning change that needs to be reported immediately.

q: A patient suddenly develops chest pain and difficulty breathing. What should the LPN do first?
options: Finish current tasks, then check on the patient
Stay with the patient, ensure safety, and call for help immediately
Ask the patient to walk to the nurses' station
Wait to see if the symptoms pass on their own
rationale: A sudden, serious change like chest pain and difficulty breathing is an emergency. The LPN should stay with the patient, keep them safe, and get help right away rather than managing it alone.

q: Which is an early, sometimes subtle, sign of shock?
options: A significant drop in blood pressure
Anxiety, cool skin, and a faster-than-usual heart rate
Complete loss of consciousness
Clearly low urine output over several hours
rationale: Early shock can be subtle: the body compensates, so anxiety, cool skin, and a faster heart rate may appear before blood pressure clearly drops.

q: A patient with heart failure develops increasing shortness of breath, leg swelling, and a 4-pound weight gain in two days. What does this suggest?
options: Normal, expected findings needing no action
Possible fluid buildup that should be reported
Dehydration that requires more fluids
A sign the patient is recovering well
rationale: Rapid weight gain with increasing shortness of breath and swelling suggests fluid retention, a warning sign in heart failure that should be reported promptly.

q: For a patient with diabetes, which symptom set needs the fastest response?
options: Increased thirst and frequent urination over several days
Sweating, shakiness, and sudden confusion
Mild fatigue after a large meal
Slightly elevated blood sugar on a routine check
rationale: Sweating, shakiness, and sudden confusion suggest low blood sugar, which can become dangerous quickly and needs fast treatment. High blood sugar symptoms develop more gradually.

q: A patient with COPD reports more difficulty breathing and a change in sputum color. What should the LPN do?
options: Consider this a normal daily variation and take no action
Report the change, since it may indicate a worsening condition or infection
Encourage the patient to exercise more to strengthen the lungs
Restrict the patient's fluids
rationale: A change in breathing difficulty or sputum color/amount in a COPD patient can indicate a worsening condition or infection and should be reported.

q: After a burn injury, what is an early priority for the nurse?
options: Applying ice directly to the burn
Moving the patient from the source of the burn and assessing breathing
Wrapping the burn tightly with a bandage immediately
Offering food and water right away, before anything else
rationale: Early priorities after a burn are moving the patient away from the source and assessing breathing, especially if the face or airway may be affected by heat or smoke.

q: What does a change in level of consciousness in a previously stable patient most often indicate?
options: A normal part of aging with no significance
A possible serious problem that needs prompt evaluation
That the patient is simply tired and needs rest only
Nothing significant if vital signs are unchanged
rationale: A change in level of consciousness is one of the most important warning signs of a serious, developing problem and should always be reported promptly.

q: When should the LPN attempt to independently manage a rapidly worsening, unstable patient rather than call for help?
options: Whenever the LPN feels confident about the situation
Never — an unstable, worsening patient should always prompt an immediate call for help
Only during night shift when fewer staff are available
Only if the RN is busy with another patient
rationale: The LPN's role in a rapidly worsening or unstable situation is to stay with the patient, keep them safe, and call for help immediately — not to manage it independently.

q: An LPN notices a coworker charting a medication as given before actually administering it. What should the LPN do?
options: Say nothing since it's not the LPN's business
Report the concern by following the facility's chain of command
Confront the coworker angrily in front of patients
Change the chart entry themselves
rationale: Patient safety and accurate documentation must be addressed through the proper chain of command, not ignored or handled unprofessionally.

q: Which best describes 'continuity of care'?
options: Providing consistent, coordinated care across settings and providers
Only providing care during one single shift
Charting once a day
Working only with the RN and no other discipline
rationale: Continuity of care means a patient's care stays consistent and coordinated as they move between providers and settings.

q: A confused patient's family member, who is not the designated healthcare decision-maker, asks for detailed information about the patient's condition. What should the LPN do?
options: Share full details since it's family
Decline to share details and refer them to the RN or provider per privacy policy
Give a brief summary since they seem concerned
Ask the patient's roommate for permission
rationale: Not every family member is automatically authorized to receive protected health information; confirm authorization before sharing anything.

q: What is the main purpose of a case manager on the healthcare team?
options: To coordinate services and continuity of care for complex patients
To administer all of a patient's medications
To replace the need for a physician
To handle only billing questions
rationale: A case manager coordinates services, resources, and continuity of care, especially for patients with complex needs.

q: An LPN is asked to perform a task outside their scope of practice. What is the correct response?
options: Attempt it carefully to help the team
Politely decline and notify the RN or supervisor
Ask a UAP to perform it instead
Do it quietly if no one is watching
rationale: Practicing outside one's scope risks patient safety and licensure; the correct response is to decline and notify a supervisor.

q: Which is the best example of properly using the chain of command?
options: Yelling at a physician in front of patients
Reporting a persistent unsafe situation to a nursing supervisor when it isn't resolved
Ignoring unsafe situations to avoid conflict
Posting concerns about a coworker on social media
rationale: The chain of command exists so unresolved safety concerns are escalated appropriately, not ignored or handled unprofessionally.

q: Which of the following best reflects patient advocacy?
options: Making all treatment decisions for a confused patient without input
Speaking up for a patient's expressed wishes and rights
Only doing whatever the family requests
Avoiding involvement in patient care decisions
rationale: Advocacy means representing and supporting the patient's own expressed wishes and rights within the care team.

q: Which patient is at greatest risk for skin breakdown?
options: A patient who is fully mobile and independent
A patient who is incontinent, immobile, and has poor nutrition
A healthy young adult with no chronic conditions
A patient who ambulates independently every day
rationale: Incontinence, immobility, and poor nutrition are major combined risk factors for pressure injury and skin breakdown.

q: A needlestick injury occurs while caring for a patient. What is the first step?
options: Ignore it if it seems minor
Wash the area immediately with soap and water, then report the exposure per policy
Wait until the end of the shift to report it
Only mention it informally to a coworker
rationale: Immediate washing and prompt formal reporting are essential to reduce infection risk and start any needed follow-up care.

q: Which is an example of medical (clean) asepsis, rather than surgical (sterile) asepsis?
options: Sterile gloving for a wound dressing change
Routine handwashing between patients
Opening and maintaining a sterile field
Using sterile instruments for an invasive procedure
rationale: Medical asepsis (clean technique) reduces the number of microorganisms, such as routine handwashing; surgical asepsis eliminates all microorganisms from a specific area.

q: What should be done for a patient identified as an aspiration risk during meals?
options: Leave them fully reclined during meals
Sit them upright and supervise meals closely
Rush the meal to reduce the time at risk
Give only liquids and never any solid food
rationale: Sitting upright and supervising closely reduces the risk of choking and aspiration during meals.

q: Which room placement is safest for a confused patient who is prone to wandering?
options: A room far from the nurses' station with the door closed
A room near the nurses' station with regular checks
A room with the bed raised to its highest position
A dark, quiet room with minimal supervision
rationale: Placing a wandering-risk patient near the nurses' station with frequent checks allows staff to notice and respond quickly.

q: When should hand hygiene be performed?
options: Only before touching a patient
Only after touching a patient
Before and after every patient contact, and after removing gloves
Only once per shift
rationale: Hand hygiene should be performed before and after every patient contact, and always after glove removal, to prevent the spread of infection.

q: What is an appropriate safety measure for a patient on seizure precautions?
options: Keep the bed raised to its highest position
Pad the side rails and keep the bed in a low position
Restrain the patient's limbs at all times
Remove all oxygen and suction equipment from the room
rationale: Padded side rails and a low bed position reduce injury risk if a seizure occurs; suction and oxygen should stay available, not be removed.

q: Which best describes primary prevention?
options: Treating a disease that has already developed
Preventing disease before it occurs, such as through vaccination
Rehabilitating a patient after an illness
Screening for early signs of disease
rationale: Primary prevention aims to prevent disease before it starts, such as vaccination or health education.

q: Which best describes secondary prevention?
options: Vaccinating a healthy child
Screening for early detection of disease, such as a blood pressure check
Treating an already-diagnosed chronic illness
Providing hospice care
rationale: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection through screening, to catch disease before it progresses.

q: What developmental task is central to Erikson's 'trust versus mistrust' stage?
options: A toddler learning independence
An infant developing a basic sense of trust through consistent caregiving
An adolescent forming their identity
An older adult reflecting on their life
rationale: Trust versus mistrust is the infant stage, where consistent, responsive caregiving builds a basic sense of trust.

q: Which is a healthy aging practice to reinforce with an older adult?
options: Avoiding all physical activity
Staying socially engaged and physically active as tolerated
Skipping regular checkups after age 65
Limiting all social contact
rationale: Staying socially engaged and physically active, as tolerated, supports healthy aging and overall wellbeing.

q: What is important to reinforce about childhood immunizations?
options: They should only be given if the child is currently sick
Following the recommended schedule helps prevent serious childhood diseases
They are optional and rarely necessary
They should be delayed until adulthood
rationale: Following the recommended immunization schedule is an important part of preventing serious childhood illnesses.

q: Which best supports reinforcing breastfeeding education for a new mother?
options: Discouraging skin-to-skin contact
Reinforcing frequent feeding based on the newborn's hunger cues
Recommending a strict 4-hour feeding schedule for all newborns
Avoiding all support since breastfeeding is natural
rationale: Reinforcing feeding based on the newborn's own cues, rather than a rigid schedule, supports successful breastfeeding.

q: Which lifestyle factor is most linked to preventing chronic disease?
options: Avoiding all exercise
Maintaining a balanced diet, regular activity, and not smoking
Sleeping less than 4 hours nightly
Skipping regular health screenings
rationale: A balanced diet, regular physical activity, and avoiding tobacco are foundational to preventing chronic disease.

q: A patient from a different cultural background declines a treatment for personal or cultural reasons. What is the best nursing response?
options: Insist that they comply anyway
Respect their autonomy and notify the RN/provider to discuss options
Refuse to continue caring for the patient
Ignore their concerns and proceed with treatment
rationale: Patients have the right to decline treatment; the nurse respects that autonomy while ensuring the RN/provider is aware to discuss alternatives.

q: What is 'active listening'?
options: Interrupting to give advice quickly
Fully concentrating on and thoughtfully responding to what the patient says
Multitasking while the patient is talking
Only listening to part of what is said
rationale: Active listening means giving full attention and responding thoughtfully, which helps the patient feel heard and understood.

q: Which behavior might suggest a patient is coping poorly with a new diagnosis?
options: Asking questions about their condition
Complete withdrawal and refusal to discuss the diagnosis at all
Seeking support from family
Wanting more information about treatment
rationale: Complete withdrawal and refusal to engage at all can be a sign of poor coping and should be noted and reported.

q: What is the best approach when a patient becomes verbally aggressive?
options: Respond with equal aggression
Stay calm, ensure safety, and try to de-escalate the situation
Ignore the patient completely
Leave the unit immediately without informing anyone
rationale: Staying calm, ensuring safety, and using de-escalation techniques is the safest and most therapeutic approach.

q: Which is an appropriate nursing action for a patient experiencing intense, acute anxiety?
options: Leave them alone to calm down on their own
Stay with the patient and speak in a calm, reassuring manner
Overwhelm them with a lot of information at once
Tell them to simply stop worrying
rationale: Staying present with a calm, reassuring manner helps a patient in acute anxiety feel safer and more supported.

q: What best describes appropriate 'boundaries' in a therapeutic nurse-patient relationship?
options: Being close personal friends with the patient outside of work
Maintaining a professional relationship focused on the patient's needs
Sharing extensive personal details with patients
Avoiding all conversation with patients
rationale: A therapeutic relationship stays professional and centered on the patient's needs, without personal boundary-crossing.

q: A dying patient's family is present and visibly distressed. What is a supportive nursing action?
options: Avoid the family entirely to give them space
Offer a calm presence, clear information, and privacy as needed
Tell the family not to cry in the room
Rush the family out of the room
rationale: Offering calm presence, honest information, and privacy supports the family during a difficult time.

q: What is the purpose of range-of-motion (ROM) exercises for an immobile patient?
options: To increase pain intentionally
To help maintain joint flexibility and prevent contractures
To replace the need for repositioning
To cause muscle atrophy
rationale: ROM exercises help maintain joint flexibility and prevent contractures in patients who cannot move independently.

q: A patient reports pain. What is an appropriate initial nursing action?
options: Assume the patient is exaggerating
Assess the pain using a pain scale and gather more detail
Ignore it until the next scheduled check
Give a medication without any assessment first
rationale: Pain should always be assessed (location, severity, quality) before deciding on an intervention.

q: Which non-pharmacological comfort measure can help with mild pain or anxiety?
options: Loud noise and bright lights
Relaxation techniques, such as deep breathing or a quiet environment
Skipping meals
Isolating the patient completely
rationale: Relaxation techniques and a calm environment are simple, effective non-drug comfort measures.

q: What is important when providing oral hygiene for an unconscious patient?
options: Position them flat on their back
Position them on their side to help prevent aspiration
Use large amounts of liquid without suction available
Skip oral care entirely
rationale: A side-lying position during oral care helps prevent fluid or secretions from being aspirated into the airway.

q: A patient needs help with toileting and has limited mobility. What is a safe approach?
options: Rush the patient to reduce time spent
Provide privacy, use assistive devices, and ensure safety during the transfer
Leave the patient alone regardless of their ability
Withhold assistance to promote independence, even if unsafe
rationale: Providing privacy, using assistive devices, and ensuring a safe transfer protects the patient from injury while respecting dignity.

q: What is an appropriate comfort measure for a patient with dry, fragile skin?
options: Hot water baths daily
Applying moisturizer and using mild soap less frequently
Avoiding all moisturizer
Frequent hot showers
rationale: Moisturizer and gentler, less frequent soap use help protect dry, fragile skin from further breakdown.

q: Which best supports adequate rest and sleep for a hospitalized patient?
options: Grouping care activities to allow uninterrupted rest periods
Waking the patient every hour for unnecessary checks
Keeping bright lights on at all times
Providing caffeine before bedtime
rationale: Grouping necessary care tasks together helps protect longer, uninterrupted periods of rest for the patient.

q: What should the nurse do before administering a medication through a feeding tube?
options: Skip checking tube placement to save time
Verify tube placement per facility policy before administering
Crush all medications regardless of their type
Give the medication quickly without any checks
rationale: Verifying tube placement before administration is a key safety step to prevent the medication (and feedings) from entering the lungs.

q: Which is an important consideration with antihypertensive (blood pressure) medications?
options: Give the dose regardless of the current blood pressure reading
Check blood pressure before administering and hold if it is below the given parameters
Only give these medications at bedtime
Double the dose if blood pressure reads high
rationale: Blood pressure should be checked before giving an antihypertensive, and the dose held per the parameters given if it's already low.

q: A patient is prescribed a diuretic. What should the nurse monitor?
options: Only body temperature
Fluid balance, electrolytes, and blood pressure
Only heart rate
No additional monitoring is needed
rationale: Diuretics affect fluid and electrolyte balance and blood pressure, so these should be monitored closely.

q: What is important to teach a patient about taking a prescribed antibiotic?
options: Stop taking it as soon as they feel better
Complete the full prescribed course even if feeling better
Take double doses if a dose is missed
Share any leftover antibiotics with others if needed
rationale: Completing the full antibiotic course, even after symptoms improve, helps fully treat the infection and reduces resistance risk.

q: A patient asks why a medication needs to be taken with food. What should the nurse know?
options: It never matters when a medication is taken relative to food
Some medications are taken with food to reduce stomach upset or improve absorption
All medications must be taken on an empty stomach
Food always blocks a medication's effectiveness
rationale: Some medications are specifically timed with food to reduce GI upset or to improve how well they are absorbed.

q: Which action best reduces the risk of medication errors?
options: Administering medications quickly without double-checking
Following the medication rights and double-checking high-alert medications
Skipping patient identification checks when busy
Assuming a previous nurse's documentation is correct without verifying
rationale: Consistently following the medication rights and double-checking high-alert drugs are core safety practices that reduce errors.

q: What is an important nursing consideration when giving an intramuscular (IM) injection?
options: Always use the smallest possible needle regardless of muscle mass
Select an appropriate site and use proper technique to prevent injury
Inject quickly without regard to site selection
Avoid rotating injection sites entirely
rationale: Proper site selection and technique reduce the risk of injury, such as nerve damage, and support medication absorption.

q: Which change would be most important to report immediately?
options: A stable, unchanged blood pressure
A sudden drop in oxygen saturation from 96% to 85%
A normal temperature reading
An expected mild glucose rise after a meal
rationale: A sudden, significant drop in oxygen saturation is an urgent finding that needs immediate reporting.

q: What should be checked before a patient undergoes a procedure requiring contrast dye?
options: No special considerations are needed
Allergies to contrast/iodine and relevant kidney function history
Nothing, since allergies don't matter for this
Only the patient's meal preference
rationale: Checking for contrast/iodine allergies and kidney function history helps prevent serious complications from the dye.

q: What should the nurse monitor closely in a patient recovering from anesthesia?
options: Only their appetite
Airway, breathing, and level of consciousness
Only their visitor preferences
Only their room temperature preference
rationale: Airway, breathing, and level of consciousness are the top priorities immediately after anesthesia, when respiratory depression is a risk.

q: Which finding after a cardiac catheterization needs immediate reporting?
options: Mild soreness at the insertion site
A growing hematoma or loss of a distal pulse
Normal vital signs
The patient resting comfortably
rationale: A growing hematoma or loss of a distal pulse suggests a vascular complication and needs prompt reporting.

q: What does a significantly elevated white blood cell count often indicate?
options: Dehydration only
A possible infection or inflammatory process
Always a medication side effect
Nothing clinically significant
rationale: An elevated white blood cell count often signals infection or an inflammatory process and should be reported.

q: A patient with a new cast reports increasing pain, numbness, and pale fingers. What should the LPN do?
options: Reassure the patient this is completely normal
Report these neurovascular changes to the RN/provider immediately
Elevate the limb and wait until the next shift to mention it
Loosen the cast themselves
rationale: Increasing pain, numbness, and pallor after a cast may indicate compartment syndrome, a neurovascular emergency requiring immediate reporting.

q: Which pre-procedure check is essential before any invasive procedure?
options: Confirming informed consent is signed and NPO status if required
Only checking the patient's meal preference
Skipping identity verification if the patient seems familiar
Assuming allergy history is unchanged without asking
rationale: Confirming signed consent and required NPO status are essential safety checks before any invasive procedure.

q: A patient in septic shock would most likely show which combination of signs?
options: Fever, rapid heart rate, and low blood pressure
Slow heart rate, high blood pressure, and cool dry skin
Completely normal vital signs throughout
Only a mild headache
rationale: Septic shock typically presents with fever, tachycardia, and hypotension as the body responds to overwhelming infection.

q: Which action helps prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia in an intubated patient?
options: Keeping the head of the bed flat
Keeping the head of the bed elevated 30-45 degrees
Avoiding oral care entirely
Suctioning only once per day regardless of need
rationale: Keeping the head of the bed elevated 30-45 degrees reduces the risk of aspiration and ventilator-associated pneumonia.

q: What is typically the earliest sign of increased intracranial pressure?
options: A sudden drop in heart rate as the very first sign
A change in level of consciousness
Widening pulse pressure as the first sign
No signs occur until very late
rationale: A change in level of consciousness is usually the earliest sign of rising intracranial pressure; the Cushing triad signs appear later.

q: A patient with a recent spinal cord injury develops sudden low blood pressure and a slow heart rate. What might this indicate?
options: Normal recovery from the injury
Neurogenic shock, from loss of sympathetic nervous system tone
Simple dehydration only
An allergic reaction only
rationale: Neurogenic shock, caused by loss of sympathetic tone after spinal cord injury, presents with hypotension and bradycardia.

q: What is a key nursing priority during a patient's seizure?
options: Restraining the patient's limbs firmly
Protecting the patient from injury and maintaining a clear airway
Placing objects in the patient's mouth
Leaving the patient alone during the seizure
rationale: The priority during a seizure is protecting the patient from injury and keeping the airway clear — never restraining or placing objects in the mouth.

q: Which finding suggests a burn patient may have airway involvement?
options: A normal voice and clear breath sounds
Singed nasal hair, soot around the mouth, or hoarseness
A burn located only on the arm
Normal oxygen saturation
rationale: Singed nasal hair, facial soot, or hoarseness suggest possible airway or inhalation injury and need urgent assessment.

q: What is the priority nursing action for a patient showing early signs of anaphylaxis?
options: Wait and observe for worsening before acting
Prepare for immediate epinephrine administration and call for help
Give oral fluids first
Document the finding and reassess in an hour
rationale: Anaphylaxis can progress rapidly; the priority is preparing for immediate epinephrine administration and getting help right away.
